## Construction

Let $\zeta(a)=\sum_{d\ge1} d^{-a}$, which converges since $a>1$. Set
$$c=\frac{1}{4\zeta(a)}, \qquad x_n = \frac{1}{c}\,\{n\alpha\} = 4\zeta(a)\,\{n\alpha\},$$
where $\{t\}$ is the fractional part and $\alpha\in[0,1)$ is chosen as follows.

**Choice of $\alpha$.** Let $\|t\|$ denote the distance from $t$ to the nearest integer. We want $\alpha$ with
$$\|d\alpha\| \ge c\,d^{-a} \quad \text{for all integers } d\ge 1.$$
For fixed $d$, the set $B_d=\{\alpha\in[0,1):\|d\alpha\|<c\,d^{-a}\}$ has measure $2c\,d^{-a}$. This is because $d\alpha \bmod 1$ covers $[0,1)$ exactly $d$ times as $\alpha$ runs over $[0,1)$, so the set of $\alpha$ within $\varepsilon$ of a multiple of $1/d$ has total length $d\cdot 2\varepsilon/d = 2\varepsilon$. Therefore
$$\Big|\bigcup_{d\ge1} B_d\Big| \le \sum_{d\ge1} 2c\,d^{-a} = 2c\,\zeta(a) = \tfrac12 < 1.$$
So there exists $\alpha\in[0,1)$ outside every $B_d$, and it satisfies $\|d\alpha\|\ge c\,d^{-a}$ for all $d\ge1$.

**Boundedness.** Since $0\le\{n\alpha\}<1$, we have $|x_n|\le 1/c = 4\zeta(a)$ for all $n\ge 0$.

**The separation inequality.** Let $i\ne j$ be nonnegative integers and $d=|i-j|\ge1$. Put $t=\{i\alpha\}-\{j\alpha\}$. Then $|t|<1$ and $t\equiv \pm d\alpha \pmod 1$, so $|t|\ge \|d\alpha\|$. Hence
$$|x_i-x_j| = \frac{|t|}{c} \ge \frac{\|d\alpha\|}{c} \ge \frac{c\,d^{-a}}{c} = d^{-a},$$
which gives $|x_i-x_j|\,|i-j|^a \ge 1$.

So the bounded sequence $x_n = 4\zeta(a)\{n\alpha\}$, with $\alpha$ chosen as above, has the required property.

ANSWER: $x_n = 4\zeta(a)\,\{n\alpha\}$, where $\zeta(a)=\sum_{d\ge1}d^{-a}$ and $\alpha\in[0,1)$ satisfies $\|d\alpha\|\ge d^{-a}/(4\zeta(a))$ for all integers $d\ge1$ (such $\alpha$ exists because the bad sets have total measure $\le 1/2$).
